support_scope: Bounded question, all three requested legs now have retrieved passages. Passage support is separated from whole-claim support: the retrieved passages establish (a) a dated divine horned/pointed-cap identification with hierarchy-proportional horns, (b) the deity-versus-king distinction including the documented problematic cases, and (c) dated later Neo-Hittite comparators plus an earlier pre-Hittite-period headgear-object context. basis: Round-8 live re-check of the R6-05-B residual on 2026-10-17, prioritizing primary and scholarly passages. (1) Main source: the entry-cited Wikipedia Yazilikaya page was re-fetched (HTTP 200, sha256 939565a7...); the round-6 target sentence 'The left wall shows a procession of male deities, wearing the traditional kilts, pointed shoes and horned hats.' and the Chamber B caption 'the god Sharruma and King Tudhaliya IV, dated to around 1250-1220 BCE' remain visible. (2) The round-6 limit 'royal-cap contrast ... not inspected' is closed by the Bonatz IDD chapter (fetched PDF, page-verified): it states the horned pointed cap as 'the typical headgear of Hittite deities since the Old Kingdom', gives the rank gradient (single vs multiple horns), and contrasts Tuthaliya IV on Yazilikaya relief nos. 64 and 81 with the sun god on relief no. 34 - 'Both wear the long robe and rounded skullcap ... distinguished only by different hieroglyphic inscriptions and the winged sun disc'. (3) The deity/king identification leg is documented, not smoothed over: the same chapter states 'the distinction between god and king often remains problematic' (Hatip Kurunta relief with two scholarly readings), and that the crown prince Urhi-Teshub's seal impressions show a living royal figure 'wearing the high pointed horned cap and embraced by the god Sharruma'. (4) The later Neo-Hittite comparator leg is dated twice and evidenced at object level: Malatya Lion Gate reliefs (late 12th or 11th cent.) where the ruler wears 'either a high conical double-horned crown or a rounded skull-shaped hairstyle' with the difference read as altered status; Ivriz (Warpalawa in power 738-710 BCE; god in horned helmet, king smaller, with Hawkins' translation of the Luwian inscription); and the Carchemish III primary report, where a horned crown survives as find B. 63a, a deity slab carries it (B. 49c), and a figure without it is argued to be a mortal priestess. (5) The earlier-comparator leg is partially served by dated pre-Hittite-period Alaca Hoyuk royal-tomb goods (gold diadems, 3rd millennium BCE) and by the chapter's Old Kingdom 16th-cent. seal comparator; no Hattic-period headgear image was retrieved (sweep recorded). (6) Textual-term and textual-description layers were added: KBo 15.15 (via Kummel 1967: 136-137 in an Istanbul University thesis) gives the king's statue a cap ('kalot') and 'Hatti-style shoes'; Oreshko 2018 documents Hittite kupahi 'a headgear' with Hurrian kuwahi. Every retrieval carries URL, HTTP status, byte count and sha256 of the fetched artifact; the entry file is byte-unchanged (sha256 5a2a3981a11f19500a224daf53a714d62624db4ac90eb17f9858b184cf1ddf84, identical to the round-6 baseline).
limits: Retained and new limits. (1) Seeher 2011 (the entry's cited visual authority, bibliography line 28) remains uninspected at plate level; the strongest new visual evidence is a scholarly synthesis and a monument database, not the plates. (2) No Hattic-period headgear image was retrieved; the earlier-comparator leg rests on pre-Hittite-period Alaca Hoyuk tomb jewelry (diadems) and an Old Kingdom seal comparator, and the 'Hattian' ethnic attribution of Alaca's Early Bronze Age tombs is a modern convention used by the sources cited here, not something this receipt verifies. (3) KBo 15.15 is quoted through a Turkish dissertation citing Kummel 1967: 136-137; the cuneiform autograph and the cited editions were not read, and the Hittite word behind the Turkish 'kalot' was not retrieved. (4) The British Museum collection record and the Bonnet-Ridotto PDF both returned HTTP 403 (documented); a search-result snippet from the blocked PDF was deliberately not used as a passage. (5) The Carchemish III passages come from an OCR'd Internet Archive scan; page numbers were resolved from page headers and the printed page marker for B. 63a (p. 174), and OCR artifacts are flagged where they affect the quoted text ('i66' for 166; 'leavings' for 'living ones'; 'B. 636'/'B. 63a'). (6) Dating: the Carchemish and Ivriz material is Neo-Hittite/Iron Age and the Malatya reliefs are dated late 12th-11th cent.; none of it may be projected back onto the Empire period as a Late Bronze Age witness, which is exactly the entry's line 49 terminology trap and the question's comparator requirement. (7) Passage support is kept separate from whole-claim support: the three requested legs (dated identification, deity/king distinction, comparators) are now passage-confirmed, while the entry's plate-level garment claims and its exact 'rounded cap' wording versus the scholarly 'rounded skullcap' remain open.
